title: Impacts of Artificial Lighting on Human Behaviour In-Office Buildings—A Systematic Literature Review
authors: Mohamed Salaheldin Amin Mohamed and Eziaku Onyeizu Rasheed, 2024
review_question: To examine the effects of artificial lighting on office workers and provide a comprehensive overview of the existing research, including all factors, and explore how lighting can impact various aspects of workplace behaviour, such as productivity, mood, and health.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Inclusion: Recent articles (Jan 2018-Apr 2023), English, Scopus database, empirical studies, transparent data collection/analysis, dependent variables directly measuring physical/psychological/social well-being, independent variables related to artificial lighting. Exclusion: Non-administrative office settings (mining, healthcare, factories), theoretical/technological/non-empirical papers, studies lacking transparent methods, dependent variables focused on job satisfaction/motivation, independent variables unrelated to artificial lighting (e.g., natural light).

synthesis_conclusions: Fluorescent and LED lighting are the primary types of artificial lighting influencing worker productivity in office buildings.

LED lighting demonstrates superiority over fluorescent lighting in enhancing worker performance and productivity due to its innovative features and potential benefits on circadian rhythm regulation, emotional responses, cognitive performance, and visual comfort.

Optimizing correlated colour temperature (CCT) to align with cooler colours, reducing glare through proper lighting design, and ensuring high colour rendering index (CRI) values can collectively enhance worker productivity and well-being.
Maintaining appropriate illuminance levels, considering both intensity and quality, fosters optimal performance and positive employee experiences.
Dynamic lighting control has potential for cognitive performance enhancement and positive impact on mood and alertness.
Lighting plays a vital role in circadian rhythms, sleep patterns, and preventing health issues.
evidence_gaps: Small sample sizes and limited participant diversity in many studies, making generalization difficult.
Lack of consideration for temporal variables (e.g., morning vs. afternoon) affecting working memory.
Insufficient distinction between sunlight and artificial light during illuminance measurements in some studies.
Insufficient deep study on the impact of lighting glare and Colour Rendering Index (CRI) on human behaviour, visual performance, and comfort.
Ethical considerations and experimental design issues need further addressing.
heterogeneity_sources: Differences in experimental techniques, model approaches, and conditions across studies.
Variations in sample sizes and participant diversity.
limitations: The review focused solely on peer-reviewed articles from a single database (Scopus).
Future research could benefit from broadening the scope to include other types of academic work (e.g., doctoral dissertations, research reports).
Using more specialized databases (e.g., Web of Science Core Collection, PsycINFO, PubMed) could yield more extensive results.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Artificial light characteristics (spectrum, intensity, timing) influence human physiological rhythms, affecting alertness, sleep, and mood in office environments.
Lighting characteristics (e.g., color temperature, brightness, glare) impact human perception of space, comfort, and aesthetic appeal, influencing psychological well-being and performance.

mechanism_chain.description: The review synthesizes various causal mechanisms by which artificial lighting impacts human well-being and performance in office settings, including physiological and perceptual pathways.
